title: KiBa-Pro brings AI to battery cell manufacturing - electrive.com
content:
How can data and artificial intelligence transform the battery cell production of tomorrow? This is the question addressed by the joint project KiBa-Pro, which launched in July 2026 under the leadership of EAS Batteries.
Symbolic image
Backed by €2.4 million in funding from the German Federal Government, the project brings together research institutions and industry partners to develop a new data-driven approach to manufacturing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells.
The consortium combines expertise from across the battery value chain. EAS Batteries is coordinating the project and leading the digitalisation of cell manufacturing, while RWTH Aachen is responsible for cell characterisation and the development of AI models. KIT and Batalyse are focusing on research data management, automated analysis of measurement data and the digital product passport at cell level. Associated partner Omron is contributing automation and data acquisition solutions.
As a first step, EAS Batteries will fully digitalise its production line. Additional sensors and modern interfaces will systematically capture production, material and quality data, which will then be consolidated in a central data infrastructure. The aim is to establish a seamless data foundation across the entire production process.
The consortium will use this data to develop a virtual LFP battery cell. Advanced AI methods will analyse large datasets to identify correlations between production parameters and resulting cell properties. This will enable precise evaluation of factors such as layer thickness, porosity, material throughput and temperature profiles.
The aim is to predict the effects on service life, capacity and performance before physical production trials begin. This will allow the consortium to simulate and evaluate process optimisations virtually before implementing them in production, reducing development effort and scrap rates, accelerating optimisation cycles and enabling potential issues to be identified at an early stage. At the same time, the project is laying the groundwork for future requirements such as the digital product passport.
The project partners plan to gradually integrate the results of KiBa-Pro into industrial production.

title: Europe misses out on billion-euro battery cell profits - electrive.com
content:
Europe's dependence on Asian - particularly Chinese - battery cell manufacturers like CATL continued to deepen in 2025. 77 per cent of EV battery were produced in Asia, up from 70 per cent in 2024. Many of the cells produced in Europe also come from Asian companies.
Cell production at PowerCo in Salzgitter (symbolic image)
Image: PowerCo
A recent Deloitte study reveals that European companies in the automotive and battery sectors are missing out on billions in revenue due to Asian dominance in the battery value chain. Specifically, European battery companies could lose out on profits totalling €10.5 billion over the next four years if they do not produce the battery cells required for EVs manufactured in Europe themselves. According to Deloitte: when accounting for imported precursors, production facilities, and skilled workers dispatched from Asia – on which the European battery industry relies – the lost value added could even reach €100 to €150 billion by 2030.
Some European corporations have considered large-scale investments in battery cell production in recent years but have often hesitated. For instance, Bosch CEO Stefan Hartung admitted in January
in an interview with
: “The risk was simply too great: to play a relevant role, we would have had to invest double-digit billions. And we have seen how some promising European projects have unfortunately failed spectacularly.” This likely refers, among others, to the bankruptcy of the Swedish company
Northvolt
, in which VW and BMW had placed their bets.
Meanwhile, the European Union has recognised the importance of battery cell production for traction batteries in European-made EVs and has just published a call for funding under its ‘
Battery Booster
‘ initiative. This programme aims to provide interest-free loans to support the scaling-up of cell factories. The projects most likely to benefit are those by
(a joint venture by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and TotalEnergies),
(backed by Renault, among others), and
(part of the VW Group). If these cell factories succeed in ramping up production, a battery cell industry under European ownership could finally emerge.
While cell factories already exist in Europe, most are under Asian ownership, such as the plant operated by the Chinese company
CATL in Arnstadt near Erfurt
. The Deloitte study notes that while Europe accounts for 13 per cent of global cell factory market share, 98 per cent of its production capacity was controlled by Asian manufacturers in 2025.
Harald Proff, Global Automotive Sector Leader at Deloitte, explains why it is crucial for European companies to strengthen their position in the battery value chain: “Batteries determine the range, performance, and price of an electric vehicle. If European manufacturers are not competitive in this area, sales will come under even greater pressure. The industry and policymakers must now work together to reduce dependence, particularly on China.”
According to Deloitte, the majority of battery value added is generated during material extraction and processing (50 to 60 per cent) and cell production (15 to 30 per cent). These stages significantly influence the economic viability and stability of downstream processes. However, European battery companies are currently not sufficiently positioned in these areas: for 83 per cent of the surveyed companies, producing cell components is a key challenge, followed by material extraction and processing (82 per cent).
Nevertheless, there are now promising projects in Germany and Europe for material extraction and processing, such as the planned lithium extraction in the Upper Rhine Valley and processing in Frankfurt-Höchst
, starting in 2028.

title: Leclanché in fresh bid to delay annual report as funding talks continue – Batteries International
content: Swiss energy storage group Leclanché is asking regulators for another extended deadline for publication of its annual results — saying it was not yet able to show its ability to operate as a going concern through at least June 2027. The troubled company said on August 3 it had filed the latest request with SIX Exchange Regulation (SER), which regulates and monitors exchange participants and issuers on the Swiss Stock Exchange. The application came just weeks after Leclanché secured a temporary exemption from publishing its 2025 annual report — originally due by July 31. Six said on June 1 it was temporarily suspending shares trading in Leclanché until the report was released. In its latest request to SER, Leclanché said discussions with a new strategic partner about potential additional funding and support to reinforce its going concern assessment through to June 2027 were taking longer than expected. SER had yet to announce its decision as of August 3. Batteries International reported in June 2025 that Leclanché was pushing ahead with efforts “to achieve and maintain a positive equity position” and to demonstrate the firm’s ability to continue as a going concern through at least June 2026. The company had said previously that it was in a situation of negative equity as of the end of 2024. Leclanché appointed Jens Emrich as CFO effective March 1 this year. Emrich was most recently a senior executive at Li-Cycle Europe — part of the troubled lithium ion battery recycling group that was acquired by mining giant Glencore in 2025. The appointment was announced five days after Leclanché said it had concluded a financing arrangement with strategic partners in the amount of CHF 16.7 million ($22 million) to support its near-term operational requirements. title: Battery industry expands beyond vehicles
content:
Market Analysis
Battery Applications
Battery Manufacturing
Interviews
Slowing EV growth pushed manufacturers to diversify into utility storage, data centers, robotics and military applications nationwide.
August 4, 2026
8 Min Read
What was formerly the BlueOval SK Battery Park plant in Kentucky, constructed to build EV batteries, is now wholly owned by Ford and will make energy storage system batteries.
Ford Motor Co.
At a Glance
Federal incentives drove $127 billion in U.S. battery projects, creating over 131,000 jobs nationwide.
U.S. energy storage capacity hit 137 GWh in 2025, with 43 percent growth projected for next year.
Military battery market valued at $2.57 billion in 2026, expected to exceed $5.22 billion by 2034.
Driven initially by the rapid rise of electric vehicles, the battery industry has evolved into a far more complex and strategically vital sector. Lithium-ion technology remains the foundation, but demand now extends across energy systems, defense, and industrial automation. The most successful manufacturers are those that built flexible facilities capable of serving multiple markets. Those early investments are now being repurposed to support a broader and more resilient energy transition.
The demand surge
The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 triggered an unprecedented wave of U.S. battery investment. Federal incentives helped drive more than $127 billion in announced projects within two years, spanning over 225 developments and more than 131,000 projected jobs. A new “
Battery Belt
” emerged across the Midwest and Southeast, anchored by large facilities such as Ultium Cells in Ohio and LG Chem in Tennessee.
Related:
AGM Batteries Dominate Modern Cars as Electronics and Start-Stop Systems Drive Market Shift
Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina. Credit: Toyota.
In response to aggressive project timelines, engineering firms have played a pivotal role in supporting the design and commissioning of thousands of gigawatt-hours (GWh) of lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. This work spans the full battery value chain, from electrode and cathode production to cell formation and pack assembly.
As the market shifted
The response was a shift toward diversification. Manufacturers began aligning production capacity with multiple sectors rather than relying solely on automotive demand.
LG Energy Solution's LFP ESS battery facility opened in Holland, MI in May 2025.
New demand vectors
As the battery market diversifies beyond electric vehicles, demand is now driven by a broad array of sectors, each with unique requirements and growth trajectories. This expansion creates new opportunities and challenges for manufacturers, necessitating flexible production approaches that can serve the distinct needs of emerging applications. Below are some of the fastest growing demand vectors reshaping the industry landscape.
Utility-scale energy storage
The electric grid has quickly become the largest new source of battery demand. In 2025, the U.S. added 58 GWh of utility-scale energy storage, reaching 137 GWh total capacity. Demand is projected to grow another 43 percent in 2026, driven by renewable integration and grid reliability needs. By early 2026, domestic manufacturing capacity for battery storage systems matched 100 percent of U.S. demand for the first time.
Related:
10 Exciting EV Battery Stocks in 2026
Automakers have responded with major investments. Ford committed $2 billion to convert its Kentucky EV battery plant into a BESS production hub targeting 20 GWh annually. Tesla and General Motors have also expanded into grid-scale storage. These applications rely heavily on LFP chemistry for its longevity and safety profile.
Hyperscale data centers
The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has transformed data centers into major energy drivers. The U.S. data center energy storage market reached approximately $1 billion in 2025 and is growing at over 6.5 percent annually. Operators are deploying lithium-ion Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) systems and onsite storage to ensure reliability and manage power demand.
AI data center. Credit: Hugo Kurk / iStock via Getty Images
Energy storage deployment surged in early 2026 as data centers added battery systems to mitigate grid stress and ensure uptime. These applications closely align with EV battery manufacturing capabilities, allowing existing facilities to transition into this market.
Department of Defense
Battery technology has become a national security priority. The Department of Defense outlined its Lithium Battery Strategy 2023–2030 and is preparing a broader update under the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act. The updated framework
emphasizes domestic supply chains and system standardization
Military demand is expanding across unmanned systems, electrified platforms, and advanced field equipment. The military battery market is valued at $2.57 billion in 2026 and is projected to exceed $5.22 billion by 2034. Applications require high energy density, reliability, and performance under extreme conditions.
Battery-powered military tactical drone. Credit: Shcherbak Volodymyr/iStock / Getty Images Plus
Robotics and autonomous systems
Beyond the grid and the battlefield,
robotics and autonomous systems
represent a growing and structurally important source of lithium-ion demand. The global robot battery market reached approximately $4.8 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow to $11.6 billion by 2034, with lithium-ion technologies accounting for more than 62 percent of the segment.
This growth is driven by rapid deployment across logistics, manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, and commercial services. Autonomous mobile robots and automated systems are becoming standard in warehouses and production environments, while service robots are expanding into healthcare and retail applications. Many of these systems operate untethered and continuously, requiring compact, high-energy-density batteries capable of long cycle life.
Industrial humanoid robots in warehouse environment demonstrating battery-powered operation. Credit: SweetBunFactory / iStock via Getty Images
Summary of demand vectors
The diversity of applications reinforces the need for varied battery solutions. Some use cases prioritize energy density, while others focus on durability, fast charging, or thermal stability. As with other emerging demand vectors, no single chemistry or configuration meets all requirements.
For manufacturers, this segment represents a fragmented but durable source of demand. Facilities designed with flexible production capabilities are best positioned to serve the evolving needs of robotics and autonomous systems.
Supply chain resilience
Despite significant domestic investment, U.S. battery manufacturing continues to rely heavily on foreign sources for key materials. The Inflation Reduction Act mandates increasing proportions of these materials to be sourced domestically or from allied countries, prompting structural shifts throughout the supply chain.
Some companies are leading efforts to close the domestic materials loop by developing recycling facilities that process battery feedstock into recovered metals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. These large-scale facilities are designed to handle tens of thousands of metric tons of battery materials annually.
In addition to recycling, advances are being made in lithium extraction projects, alongside plans for the expansion of additional recycling centers. Regional initiatives like the Critical Materials Crossroads are actively working to build domestic refining capacity and foster workforce development in this sector.
Manufacturing complexity
As recycled and multi-source materials are integrated into production, manufacturing complexity increases. Facilities must track material origin, chemistry, and processing history to meet regulatory requirements and qualify for incentives.
Feedstock segregation introduces additional challenges. Different chemistries require separate processing flows or strict cleaning protocols between runs. Variations in material composition affect performance, requiring dynamic process tuning and quality control.
Manufacturing Execution Systems must maintain full traceability at the batch level. As a result, battery plants are evolving into hybrid systems that combine production with materials management. This represents a significant departure from earlier single-product gigafactories.
How to scale confidently
Scaling from a pilot plant to full industrial production is a high-stakes leap that the most successful organizations approach as both a technical and a people-centered challenge. To navigate this complexity, teams should adopt a holistic and incremental strategy, beginning with a thorough understanding of the production process. A pilot plant must be intentionally designed to generate the precise data required for making informed full-scale decisions.
Because the impacts of early choices won’t follow a simple linear path, seemingly minor factors, such as humidity controls or other environmental requirements, can have major long-term consequences on cost and constructability. Incorporating benchmarking against similar facilities is also essential to validate assumptions related to acreage, utilities and layout, enabling teams to right-size the solution and minimize total ownership costs.
With these foundations in place, effective scale-up relies on disciplined early planning, a high-functioning project team, and a flexible program management system. Defining the project’s core values and translating them into clear KPIs that reflect long-term success is critical. Progressing through stage gates allows teams to progressively lock in decisions as design evolves, a process particularly vital when fast-tracking necessitates starting procurement and construction before design completion.
Teams should also ensure dedicated staffing, adopt a contracting strategy that encourages collaboration, and establish clear decision rights to prevent delays. Lastly, robust project controls and a formal Management of Change process are important to monitor performance, proactively manage inevitable changes, and prevent cost and schedule overruns as project complexity grows.
The road ahead
The mid-2020s buildout created a strong foundation for domestic battery manufacturing. U.S. battery production increased significantly between 2020 and 2025, and domestic manufacturing capacity for energy storage systems reached 100 percent of demand in 2026.
The challenge now lies in deploying that infrastructure across a more complex demand landscape. Leading manufacturers are treating facilities as adaptive assets capable of multi-chemistry production and rapid reconfiguration.
Global battery demand is expected to rise from approximately 1.6 TWh in 2025 to about 4.2 TWh by 2030 and 6.8 TWh by 2035, with lithium-ion technologies accounting for the majority of that growth.
The industry is no longer building toward a single outcome. It is learning to operate across multiple demand vectors simultaneously, with adaptability emerging as its most critical capability.

title: AGM Batteries Now Power Most New Vehicles
content:
Market Analysis
Automotive & Mobility
AGM technology now powers 70% of new vehicles, driven by start-stop systems, heat resistance & growing electronic demands in modern cars.
August 3, 2026
4 Min Read
The dead factory-installed AGM battery from a 2017 Ford Focus.
Dan Carney
At a Glance
AGM batteries handle deep discharge cycles from start-stop systems better than flooded batteries.
Modern vehicles now contain 150 electronic devices, up from 20 two decades ago, straining batteries.
EVs require AGM auxiliary batteries to support safety functions and over-the-air software updates.
The North American market for
12-volt lead-acid car batteries
is forecast to be nearly $10B this year,
according to MarkWide Research
. By 2035, the market is predicted to grow to more than $14B, so sales of conventional car batteries are not going anywhere, despite a shift from combustion power to electric power for propulsion.
Most of us are familiar with the traditional flooded 12-volt lead-acid batteries that cars use to start. These are the ones that you have to keep filled with distilled water that circulates between the lead plates in the battery’s cells.
There’s another, more advanced and expensive technology that is gaining ground in the 12-v car battery market, called
Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM)
. This technology started in high-end and high-performance models, but has since proliferated into mainstream and even entry-level cars.
I discovered this fact when my daughter’s 2017 Ford Focus needed a new battery after nine years of service. I was impressed that the original battery lasted so long, and then discovered the reason why when I looked up its replacement and discovered that it was a nearly $200 AGM battery and not the basic flooded lead-acid battery I expected.
I’m not the only one who thinks that AGM batteries are for expensive sports cars. The
AAA explainer on battery technology
uses an image of a Lamborghini to illustrate AGM use cases!
Chatting with Jason Fuhr, senior director for engineering at
battery manufacturer Clarios
, helped clear things up. As the AAA site describes, flooded batteries are cheaper, but shorter-lived, while AGM batteries cost more and last longer, as demonstrated by the nine-year run of the Focus’s factory-installed battery.
“In a standard flooded battery, it's the technology that's been around for a long time, and you've got the lead-acid plates that are in there that are completely immersed in the electrolyte, Fuhr explained. “The acid needs to stay above the plates, and at points in history, people were watering them, adding water to make sure that the levels were consistent and get full life out of it.”
There’s no need to add water to an AGM battery. “The separator is an absorbent glass mat, and so the acid is absorbing into that glass mat, and then there's compression on the plates, and so between that compression and the acid electrolyte being inside the separator, you get much better and more consistent performance over life,” Fuhr stated.
That’s why 70% of new cars employ AGM batteries for their 12-volt battery, according to Clarios. This is because modern cars frequently employ start/stop technology and run a lot of power-consuming electronics, reported Fuhr.
“AGM batteries are really the premier technology for start/stop, and I think that's where it started,” he said. “They're able to handle deep discharge and the cycling that's coming from start/stop applications. applications, and you know that's why a lot of the automakers have adopted and continue to adopt it for that benefit.”
Even cars that don’t rely on start/stop systems are placing greater demands on their cars’ batteries. “If you look at the trend of electronics, 20 years ago, there were maybe 20 devices, 20 hardcore electronic devices on a vehicle,” Fuhr noted. “Now we're at 150, and I think the expectation is in, the next five years, that it may double again. And because AGM batteries have lower resistance, they're able to handle those cycling loads. AGM batteries are able to charge back up again and still provide a long life, which you know is evidenced by your daughter's vehicle.”
However, a 2017 Focus isn’t really loaded with a lot of tech, so that didn’t necessarily explain why Ford would have installed a costly AGM battery in a cost-conscious model like the Focus. Fuhr suggested that perhaps it was due to the desire for a single battery in a vehicle that included versions that did use start/stop technology.
But then he hit on another AGM benefit that is one of the features on AAA’s list of flooded battery shortcomings: heat resistance. AGM batteries are more tolerant of hot environments, and the Focus is a turbocharged EcoBoost model, which has higher under-hood temperatures than a naturally aspirated car would have.
“The benefit for an AGM is in high temperature,” Fuhr said. “If you've got a high temperature under-hood, you're reducing the corrosion effects [by using an AGM battery]. You have less water loss of the battery, and so that's how you're going to have better performance in a high temperature.”
The industry shift to EVs also drives AGM demand, because the 12-volt batteries in those cars go through deep charge cycles that damage flooded batteries. “In an EV, it's an auxiliary battery,” observed Fuhr. “It's providing the support functions, and so it's going to be cycling and then probably providing some safety functionality in case of the high-voltage battery going down. It provides support for over-the-air updates, and so, the benefit of that AGM battery is it's going to be able to handle that discharge that's happening while [the car is] off and then charge it back up again as the vehicle starts driving.”

title: DOE Announces Lithium-Ion Recycling Prize Winners.
content:
Battery Recycling
Battery News
Industry Outlook
DOE awards $200,000 to eight teams advancing lithium-ion battery recycling technologies, boosting U.S. supply chain resilience and innovation.
August 3, 2026
3 Min Read
The Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Prize is funded by funded by CMEI
AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
The US Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (
announced
the winners of the Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Prize, a competition aimed at advancing innovative solutions for lithium-ion battery recycling and boosting
US supply chain
resilience. By fostering domestic innovation and reducing reliance on foreign sources for critical materials, the contest plays a pivotal role in strengthening America’s ability to produce, recycle, and reuse essential components for clean energy technologies. Eight teams have been awarded $200,000 each for their groundbreaking work in strengthening America’s battery-recycling infrastructure. These teams will now move forward to Phase IV of the competition, where their proposals will undergo further validation and evaluation.
“This contest showcases the ingenuity required to maximize the value and useful life of critical materials,” stated Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary of Energy for Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE). “DOE is proud to support these talented contestants as they turn their groundbreaking ideas into scalable solutions that will fortify our country’s critical mineral supply chains.”
Related:
Promoting innovation in battery recycling
The competition was designed to address the growing need for effective lithium-ion battery recycling technologies. Entrepreneurs, engineers, and technologists were challenged to develop solutions that could improve the collection, sorting, transportation, and processing of spent or discarded lithium-ion batteries. The goal is to ensure that critical materials, such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel, remain within the domestic supply chain, reducing reliance on foreign sources and supporting the transition to clean energy.
Track 1:
New Competitors welcomed US-based legal entities with single process ideas, partial solutions, or full concept solutions, including new participants and previous competitors. Teams could consist of individual businesses or collaborations.
Track 2:
Verified Competitors invited Phase III winners to refine their solutions with a $100,000 noncash voucher, used at American-Made Network providers to validate and demonstrate pilot-scale concepts for broader implementation.
Related:
Lithium-Ion Battery Circularity: Challenges and Opportunities

Advancing to phase IV
The Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Prize, launched in 2019, is a multi-phase competition designed to increase the recovery rates of critical materials from lithium-based batteries in the United States. In Phase IV, the eight winning teams will receive $150,000 in noncash vouchers to support the validation, evaluation, and techno-economic and life cycle analysis of their proposals. This phase will culminate in a $1 million grand prize for the overall winner, with up to $3 million distributed among up to four runner-up teams.
The competition is funded by CMEI’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office and Transportation Technologies Office and is administered by the National Lab of the Rockies. It represents a significant step forward in addressing the challenges of battery recycling and critical mineral supply chain resilience.

Competitions such as the Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Prize foster collaboration and innovation among industry leaders, researchers, and technologists; the competition is helping to build a sustainable infrastructure for battery recycling. This effort ensures that the US remains competitive in the global race for critical mineral independence.

title: Ferrero Deploys Satellite Tech for Supply Chain Transparency
content:
Ferrero Deploys Satellite Tech for Supply Chain Transparency
Prioritise Us
on Google
Ferrero uses satellite imagery to improve sustainability. Credit: Ferrero
Ferrero uses geospatial data to track ingredients across vast distances, allowing the firm to monitor environmental risks in complex agricultural networks
Ferrero has adopted satellite monitoring technology to manage its
ingredient
supply chains across multiple continents.
The company operates under a principle it calls Sacco Conosciuto, which means knowing the origin and production methods of its ingredients. This practice dates back to the company's founding in 1946.
However, Ferrero's supply chain networks now span thousands of kilometres across ecosystems where cocoa, palm oil and coffee are grown. The complexity of these networks requires technology that can provide visibility at scale.
Satellite monitoring for traceability
Ferrero uses Starling, a satellite monitoring platform created by
Defense and the Earthworm Foundation. The company has worked with Starling for 10 years to gain visibility into the landscapes where its ingredients are sourced.
Thanks to this technology, we are able to deploy monitoring across
and plantations in our supply chains, at scale. Today, Starling allows us to map and monitor around 230,000 plantations across three commodities – cocoa, palm oil and coffee – in line with EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) requirements.
Nicola Somenzi, Head of Responsible Sourcing at Ferrero
Nicola Somenzi, Head of Responsible Sourcing at Ferrero
platform
uses satellite imagery and geospatial data to track agricultural supply chains. Ferrero combines this data with input from technology experts, analysts and local partners to turn insights into decisions.
This includes engaging with suppliers, working with partners and conducting field visits to understand local conditions and farming practices. The data helps the company assess where its
ingredients
come from and identify environmental risks in the supply chain.
The company actively engages with suppliers. Credit: Ferrero
Managing environmental impact
Starling
was developed as a collaborative solution for verifying forest impact across supply chains. The platform is designed to measure environmental impact and support companies working towards deforestation-free commitments and EUDR compliance requirements.
For Ferrero, the technology provides a method to monitor how the landscapes where its plantations operate are changing. The Italian manufacturer uses the data to strengthen traceability and guide its engagement with suppliers and local partners.
Key facts
Tropical forests are home to more than half of the world’s terrestrial species, despite covering less than 10% of the Earth's land surface.
Forests absorb around 7.6 billion metric tonnes of carbon dioxide each year, helping to slow the pace of climate change.
One hectare of rainforest can contain more than 300 species of trees.
The platform gives Ferrero a way to track agricultural activities in areas that are part of natural habitats. This could mean the company can respond to environmental risks more quickly than traditional monitoring methods would allow.
According to Ferrero, the satellite monitoring technology helps build a clearer picture of how the landscapes it sources from are evolving over time.
Company portals

title: eBay Drives Ongoing Fashion Circularity in Depop Acquisition
content:
eBay Drives Ongoing Fashion Circularity in Depop Acquisition
Prioritise Us
on Google
eBay has acquired Depop in order to expand circularity throughout fashion supply chains. Credit: eBay
eBay is expanding supply chain circularity and driving sustainable logistics in the fashion industry, with a US$1.2bn acquisition of Depop
eBay has completed the acquisition of Depop for approximately US$1.2bn, combining two platforms that together handle more than 71,000 tonnes of pre-owned goods annually. The transaction extends eBay's consumer-to-consumer operations and creates a larger infrastructure for managing
secondhand fashion distribution
According to eBay, the company diverted more than 71,000 tonnes of pre-loved items from landfill in 2025. Depop has processed more than 100 million items through its platform to date.
The deal brings together two distinct logistics models that operate within the recommerce sector. Both platforms manage peer-to-peer transactions without holding inventory themselves.
eBay Pre-loved Fashion: Own Boss Wardrobe
Expanding distribution networks
The acquisition builds on eBay's sustainable fashion category, which generates more than US$10bn in annual gross merchandise volume. According to eBay, combining Depop's operations with its existing infrastructure could create what the company describes as a "distinct, community-driven platform rooted in discovery, creativity and peer-to-peer connection".
states that Depop's customer base and product pricing structure make the company a "natural complement" to its consumer-to-consumer commerce operations. The platform's fulfilment model relies on individual sellers managing their own shipping and handling.
"As a global leader in C2C and recommerce, eBay's acquisition of Depop further strengthens our C2C value proposition," says Jamie Iannone, Chief Executive Officer of eBay.
"This combines two distinct customer experiences and expands our reach with the next generation of buyers and sellers.
Jamie Lannone, CEO of eBay
"Our goal is to preserve Depop's strong brand, community and product experience, while helping the team accelerate the roadmap that is already underway and explore synergies with eBay in areas that can supercharge our combined growth potential."
Operational integration approach
According to eBay, Depop will operate as a separate business following the acquisition. The platform will retain its own branding, infrastructure and operational processes.
"Joining eBay, a company with a longstanding record of driving innovation in recommerce globally, is an exciting new chapter for Depop and our community," says Peter Semple, Chief Executive Officer of Depop.
"We've built a marketplace centred on creativity, self-expression and connection, and we're just getting started.
Peter Semple, CEO at Depop
"Depop is a natural fit with eBay and together we can accelerate our growth while continuing to deliver the unique experience our users value."
According to eBay, combining Depop's operations with its global shipping capabilities, compliance systems and service infrastructure could enhance both buyer and seller experience.
"I'm excited for our two organisations, both passionate about
circular fashion
and reshaping how people buy and sell online, to come together," adds Jessica Verdugo, Circular Fashion at eBay, on LinkedIn.
The integration allows both platforms to maintain separate fulfilment processes while potentially sharing logistics resources.
Jessica Verdugo, Circular Fashion at eBay
Managing reverse supply chains
Depop's operational model extends product lifecycles by facilitating resale rather than new production. The platform has processed more than 100 million fashion items through its distribution network.
According to Depop, more than three in five purchases on the platform prevent the purchase of a new alternative. The company's framework aligns with keeping products in use and recognising repaired, upcycled,
secondhand and surplus
The platform has established targets covering net zero emissions, operations and diversity. These goals could position the resale model as a method for
reducing manufacturing demand
within the fashion sector.
According to eBay, the company has structured its operations around recommerce, using its marketplace to extend product use cycles and reduce waste across fashion and electronics categories. More than 40% of eBay's gross merchandise volume comes from pre-loved and refurbished goods.
eBay's Refurbished programme helps to extend product lifecycles and reduce the need for environmentally costly manufacturing. Credit: eBay
Investment in distribution infrastructure
eBay's operational model helped avoid an estimated 1.6 million tonnes of carbon emissions and divert 71,000 metric tonnes of waste, according to the company. The company has established the Circular Fashion Fund to provide capital and support to businesses developing solutions for textile recycling, repair and resale.
Since launching in 2022, the programme has supported more than 25 businesses. According to
, the fund is expected to distribute US$1.9m in funding by the end of 2026.
The investment programme targets businesses that extend product lifecycles through improved reverse logistics and processing capabilities. The fund provides capital to operations that manage returned goods, repair services and material recovery systems.
The combined entity manages distribution without traditional warehousing or inventory holding. Both platforms rely on decentralised fulfilment where individual sellers handle storage and shipping.

title: Europe is betting big on a battery that runs for four days
content:
Green Energy
Electrek Green Energy Brief
Wind power
Michelle Lewis
| Aug 4 2026 - 8:55 am PT
Rendering: Ore Energy
Long-duration energy storage startup
Ore Energy
has landed what it says is the largest iron-air battery deal in continental Europe so far – and now it’s raised Series A funding. [update]
August 4 update:
Ore Energy has raised $43 million in Series A funding from Plural and HV to scale its iron-air battery technology. The funding brings the company’s total raised to more than $61 million.
The new funding will enable Ore to establish its first manufacturing facility, ahead of its target for gigawatt hour-scale manufacturing in 2028.
June 22:
The Netherlands-based company announced an agreement with Dutch energy supplier Budget Thuis to deploy 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of iron-air energy storage. The deal starts with a committed 400-megawatt-hour (MWh) first phase that Ore Energy plans to deliver in 2028.
The project is notable not only for its size but also because it’s the first iron-air storage agreement with a European energy supplier. As countries add more wind and solar power, utilities are looking for ways to store renewable energy for longer periods when weather conditions don’t cooperate.
Unlike lithium-ion batteries, which are typically designed to deliver energy over a few hours, Ore Energy’s iron-air batteries can store electricity for up to 100 hours. The technology uses iron, water, and air and is designed to help fill multi-day gaps in renewable energy generation. Modular 40-foot containers are used, which can be daisy-chained to scale capacity.
Iron-air batteries aren’t perfect. They’re bulkier and less efficient than lithium-ion batteries, so they lose more energy along the way. But for a grid-scale system that’s designed to store cheap wind and solar power for days at a time, size matters a lot less than cost. That’s where iron-air’s simple, inexpensive materials could give it an edge.
For Budget Thuis, the goal is to store excess wind power when it’s plentiful and release it back to the grid during periods when renewable generation drops and electricity prices rise.
Once installed, the system will be connected to the Dutch electricity grid using Ore Energy’s containerized battery design. The company says its batteries can be configured for storage durations ranging from 24 to 100 hours. Because the technology only uses iron, water, and air, Ore Energy says it can rely on a European supply chain and avoid many of the critical minerals used in conventional batteries.
“European grids are already curtailing clean power at scale, wasting electricity that costs billions to generate, while we stay dependent on fossil fuels to cover the gaps,” said Ore Energy cofounder and CEO Aytaç Yilmaz. “Short-duration batteries alone can’t fix this. They shift solar by a few hours, but wind-heavy European grids need storage that works across days, not hours.”
Yilmaz said the Budget Thuis project marks the next step in commercializing the company’s technology after earlier pilot projects.
Budget Thuis CEO Annemarie Buitelaar said, “For us, this is about reducing exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices while giving customers access to cleaner and more predictable electricity over time. Ore Energy has demonstrated the technology and has the expertise to deploy it, which is why we are committing to 1 GWh across our portfolio, starting with a 400 MWh first phase.”
The agreement follows two earlier grid-connected deployments from Ore Energy. In February, the company announced the completion of a pilot project with EDF in France, which it described as Europe’s first grid-connected iron-air long-duration storage pilot. Conducted between August and November 2025, the project demonstrated up to four days of energy storage under real-world utility conditions.
Ore Energy had previously deployed a grid-connected iron-air installation in Delft, the Netherlands, to test how the technology integrates with existing European grid infrastructure.
If projects like this scale successfully, they could help ensure uninterrupted renewable power, regardless of weather conditions.

title: Waymo CEO explains why Tesla’s camera-only self-driving falls short
content:
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov laid out the clearest technical case yet for why cameras alone can’t take a self-driving system to full autonomy, arguing that “weak sensing” hits a safety ceiling long before it reaches superhuman performance.
He never said the word Tesla. But camera-only is Tesla’s entire bet, and this was a direct shot at it.
The sensor debate, from someone with 220 million driverless miles
Dolgov made the comments in a talk at Y Combinator’s Startup School, walking through the lessons Waymo has learned building its driver over close to two decades. He put the sensor question on the table plainly: “there’s been a long-standing debate about what kind of sensors do you actually need for autonomous driving.”
His answer draws the line that camera-only advocates tend to skip right past. “Humans of course can drive with just eyes, so there’s that proof of existence,” he said. “If the goal were to just approximately match human performance or to build an assist product, that’s a very reasonable way to go.”
Then the catch. If you’re targeting full autonomy and strongly superhuman performance, he said, “you find that weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early.”
That’s the whole argument in a couple of sentences. Cameras can match a human. They can power a driver-assist product. Dolgov’s point is that they top out below the bar a car has to clear to drive with nobody behind the wheel.
Unless you do it for demonstration purposes in a geo-fenced area with limited speed and low availability to limit danger through less mileage.
Why Waymo runs cameras, lidar, and radar together
Waymo uses three sensing types, and Dolgov spent real time on why. Cameras give you high resolution and color, but they’re passive, and they degrade in darkness and glare. Lidar directly measures the 3D structure of the world. Radar punches through fog, rain, and snow, and reads velocity directly with Doppler. Lidar and radar are active sensors, so they see just as well in pitch darkness or straight into a blinding sunset.
This isn’t redundancy for its own sake. “These different sensing modalities, they’re not backups to each other,” Dolgov said. Each one runs its own encoder, and the data fuses into a single view of the world that he says is “vastly superior to what you get with any one sensor.”
He backed it with cases where a camera goes blind. A dust storm in Phoenix, where the camera sees almost nothing while lidar cleanly picks out a pedestrian at the roadside. People hopping a concrete barrier onto a road at night. Kids chasing dogs across a pitch-black street with no headlights or streetlights on them. In each one, the camera feed is close to useless and the lidar view is clean.
Then there’s the failure case camera-only can’t engineer its way around: something physically covering the lens. A single leaf on a sensor can bring a robot to a full stop, Dolgov said, before showing a Waymo that caught a tree branch its wipers couldn’t shake and used its other sensors to drive itself safely back to the depot.
The ‘nines’ problem
Under the sensor argument sits a math argument, and it’s the part that should worry anyone extrapolating from a camera-only demo. Reliability lives on what Dolgov called an “exponential ladder of nines.” Tesla CEO Elon Musk calls it the “march of the nines.” Getting to 90% or 99% is the easy part. Every additional nine of reliability takes roughly ten times more effort than the one before it.
So the trap is picking the technology with the fastest early ramp, the one that makes the best demo, projecting that steep slope forward, and then hitting a plateau “way before the performance that is required by your product.” A demo might need one nine. A driver-assist product needs a few. A car with kids in the back and nobody driving needs a whole stack of them.
Dolgov also pushed back on the one knock that camera-only fans always reach for: cost. Waymo is on its sixth generation of hardware, and he said each generation has drastically cut the price. Betting against sensors like lidar on today’s prices, he warned, means betting on “a number that has a fairly short shelf life.”
Where Tesla fits
Tesla is the loudest bet on the other side of this debate. It pulled radar from its cars in 2021 and dropped ultrasonic sensors in 2022, going all-in on cameras with “Tesla Vision.” Elon Musk has called lidar “a fool’s errand” and said anyone relying on it is “doomed.” Tesla’s robotaxi service, which launched in Austin in 2025, runs on cameras alone. We’ve covered the Tesla Vision versus lidar fight in depth before.
So far the results line up with the exact ceiling Dolgov described. Tesla’s own robotaxi data shows a crash rate about three times worse than human drivers, even with a human safety monitor in the front seat. Musk has claimed FSD is safer than humans, release after release, and the data hasn’t backed him up yet, even after being heavily massaged by Tesla.
Waymo is running the numbers Dolgov says camera-only can’t reach. Its latest safety report, based on 220 million rider-only miles, shows 94% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers would cause over the same distance, roughly 17 times better. Waymo is now serving around half a million paid trips a week across 15 US cities and is scaling toward a 1-million-weekly-rides target, even as Musk insists Waymo “never had a chance” against Tesla.
Tesla recently confirmed it has accumulated 380,000 driverless miles over the past year since launching its robotaxi. Waymo’s driverless service does that in a day.
Electrek’s Take
This is the most useful version of the lidar-versus-cameras argument I’ve seen, because Dolgov doesn’t pretend cameras are useless. He concedes the thing Tesla fans always lead with. Yes, humans drive with two eyes, and yes, cameras alone can build a genuinely good driver-assist product. That’s not the disagreement. The disagreement is whether “good enough to help a human drive” ever becomes “good enough to remove the human,” and his answer is no, because the sensing tops out before you get the last few nines.
Now, Tesla would point to its active Robotaxi service as an example of “removing the human”, but Dolgov also said that camera-only is also good for a demo, and that’s basically what Tesla’s Robotaxi service is right now.
Tesla just confirmed that unsupervised miles only added up to 380,000 miles to date. That’s basically a demo at low speeds in small geo-fenced areas in Texas.
Top comment by Realist
Tesla own patents on Lidar equipment, so they have studied it. History shows that a technology pioneer often doesn't grasp the significance of the thing they studied and once had a lead in...consider Xerox and the computer mouse. The first MRI manufacturer and the first CT scanner builders are now more or less out of business. There's often a 'second mover' advantage.
History also shows that tech devices tend to get radically cheaper as they mature; ABS in cars once was an option that cost over $1000. Air bags were once a pricey option. So it would be expected that lidar might follow the same cost curve as microwave ovens have.
A lot of high-end cars now have radar and lidar. Nobody is arguing that these additions make the car less safe, so why would an autonomous car with lidar be less safe than a vision-only car?
The nines framing is the part Tesla investors should sit with. Tesla has spent years on the steep, easy part of the curve, where every FSD release looks a lot better than the last, and Musk keeps drawing that slope straight up to robotaxis. Dolgov is describing precisely why that line breaks: the early gains are cheap and the tail is brutal, and the tail is the entire safety problem once you’re driving millions of miles a week.
The cost point matters too, because “lidar is too expensive” is the last technical leg the camera-only case has to stand on. Waymo’s on its sixth hardware generation and says cost is dropping fast. If sensors keep getting cheaper while camera-only keeps hitting the same wall, “cameras are the pragmatic choice” gets weaker every year.
We are hearing that Waymo is close to having its entire package (car + Waymo sensor suite and driver) at around $60,000. At that point, the fact that you have a system that works at scale is way more important than a ~$20,000 cost advantage on the car.

title: Tesla China sales are crashing as exports surge
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 4 2026 - 7:17 am PT
Tesla’s sales inside China fell 19% in the first half of 2026 compared to its peak in 2023, dropping to the lowest level in years, according to new data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA).
At the same time, exports out of Giga Shanghai surged 127%. Tesla’s China plant is increasingly building cars to ship somewhere else.
Domestic retail sales came in at 238,955 vehicles for January through June, down from 263,410 a year earlier. That’s a 9% year-over-year drop, and it’s 19% below Tesla’s first-half peak of 294,105 back in 2023.
Exports went the other way. Tesla shipped 228,994 cars out of China in the first half, up from 101,064 in 2025. Those cars go to Europe, Canada, and other Asian markets that Giga Shanghai supplies.
Tesla’s first-half China deliveries: domestic retail has fallen for three straight years while exports have more than doubled. Data: CPCA.
The wholesale number hides the problem
This is where Tesla’s China numbers get misread every single month.
Tesla and much of the financial press quote the “wholesale” figure, which is everything Giga Shanghai builds, both the cars sold to Chinese buyers and the cars loaded onto ships for export. On that basis, first-half output of 467,949 was up 28% year-over-year and just 2% shy of the 2023 record. Sounds great.
But wholesale is retail plus export. Strip out the cars leaving the country and you get what Tesla is actually selling to Chinese consumers. And that number is shrinking.
We’ve flagged this gap all year. In April,
Tesla’s reported “36% surge” was actually a 10% retail decline
once you removed exports, and
Q1 retail fell 16% behind a “rising” wholesale headline
. The first-half data confirms it wasn’t a blip.
Monthly CPCA breakdown for the first half. Retail is what Tesla sold in China; export is what it shipped out. Data: CPCA.
Exports now make up 49% of everything Giga Shanghai builds, up from 28% a year ago. Half the plant’s output no longer serves the market it was built for.
In January and April, Tesla exported more cars from China than it sold inside China. Data: CPCA.
That trend might be increasing. CPCA reported that Tesla had a record wholesale of 93,000 vehicles in July. The vast majority of those are expected to be exports.
Squeezed at home, leaning on exports
The domestic slide isn’t a mystery. Tesla is
getting squeezed by Chinese competition
, and 2025 was its first-ever annual sales decline in the country. BYD, Xiaomi, Nio, and a dozen others keep launching cheaper, newer, better-equipped EVs while the Model 3 and Model Y age.
The export boom partly reflects a low base. Tesla barely exported anything in February and March 2025 during the refreshed Model Y changeover, which is why those months show 400%-plus year-over-year gains. But even against normal months, the trend is clear: Giga Shanghai has pivoted from serving China to serving the world.
Why the split matters for a SpaceX merger
The timing is awkward for Tesla, because its China footprint just became a strategic problem.
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Tesla is weighing options for its China business, from a spinoff to an outright sale to winding it down, to clear a path for a
potential merger with SpaceX
. SpaceX is a major US defense and space contractor, and folding Tesla’s Chinese manufacturing into it would set off national-security alarms in Washington. Musk called the report “fake news.”
Whatever the label, the data reframes what a China spinoff would actually cost Tesla. If Giga Shanghai has quietly turned into an export hub feeding Europe, Canada, and Asia, then separating it doesn’t just hand away a shrinking sales market. It hands away nearly half a million cars a year of the company’s most efficient production, and the pipeline that keeps showrooms stocked on three continents.
Electrek’s Take
I have been reporting on Tesla long enough to remember that when Musk first announced Tesla Shanghai, he said it would produce cars only for the domestic Chinese market.
Boy did that turn out to be completely false.
I think Tesla is on the verge of exporting more vehicles from China than it sells in China.
It couldn’t come at a worse time as Musk is trying to merge Tesla with SpaceX. However creative the solution is, it has to take into account that Tesla giving up China is not just giving up on the largest EV market in the world, which Tesla could live with considering sales are falling in the market, but it is also giving up nearly half a million vehicle sales in other markets supplied by Giga Shanghai.

title: Audi's cheapest EV is also its most efficient car of all time
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 4 2026 - 6:55 am PT
Audi is reviving the A2 name for its new entry-level electric vehicle. With its debut just around the corner,
revealed a few more details about the new ultra-efficient EV.
Audi A2 e-tron is the brand’s most efficient car
After the original A2 first arrived over 25 years ago, it quickly became known as the “world’s first four-door three-liter car” with a combined fuel efficiency of 5.9 liters per 100 kilometers.
Audi is bringing the A2 name back, but this time it will be even more efficient with an all-electric powertrain.
Ahead of its official debut this fall, Audi revealed that the A2 e-tron will go on sale as its most efficient car ever.
“The Audi A2 has been a constant in my career ever since I joined the Volkswagen Group in the 1990s,” CEO Gernot Döllner said, adding, “This is precisely the vision we are carrying forward with the new A2 e-tron: outstanding efficiency, excellent everyday usability, and a clear understanding of what customers expect from modern electric mobility.”
Audi A2 e-tron charging (Source: Audi)
Under WLTP conditions, the Audi A2 e-tron with the 140 kW motor and efficiency package achieves an energy consumption of 12.8 kWh per 100 km.
It also has a drag coefficient of just 0.24, the best in Audi’s compact lineup. Audi said the improved efficiency is thanks to its new electric drive, batteries, and aerodynamic design.
Audi A2 e-tron (Source: Audi)
The Audi A2 e-tron features an active cool-air intake that stays closed during normal driving and at higher speeds to reduce drag. While charging or on hot summer days, the intake opens to cool and protect the battery and electronics.
Audi said the
A2 e-tron 140 kW
version is powered by a 61 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery that achieves 89.6% charging efficiency at the wallbox with an adaptive cooling strategy.
The entry-level EV is also equipped with bidirectional charging, enabling it to serve as a mobile energy bank with Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) and Vehicle-to-Home (V2H) capabilities.
Audi uses a cell-to-pack design for its LFP batteries to optimize energy density and free up more interior space.
Ahead of its official debut this fall, Audi
revealed prices
for the A2 e-tron will start at about €38,200 (about $44,000) in Germany with a WLTP driving range of up to 403 miles (649 km).
When it goes on sale this fall, the A2 e-tron will be available with four different power outputs: 125 kW, 140 kW, 170 kW, and 240 kW.
Like the new
Volkswagen ID.3 Neo
, Audi’s entry-level EV is expected to be offered with three battery packs: 50 kWh, 58 kWh, and 79 kWh. However, the A2 e-tron will deliver slightly more range at up to 403 miles (649 km).
Starting at €38,200 (about $44,000) in Germany, the A2 e-tron will arrive this fall as Audi’s most affordable EV. The Q4 e-tron starts at €47,500 ($54,00), or nearly €10,000 more than the electric A2.

has long been
one of the biggest names in premium commuter scooters, and the new MAX G3 Plus builds on that platform with a 20% larger battery rated at 717 Wh.
That boosts the claimed range to as much as 56 miles (90 miles) when ridden in lower power, while the scooter retains a 28 mph (45 km/h) top speed and a peak motor output of 2,200 watts.
One of the more interesting announcements isn’t actually about the hardware, though. Segway says the MAX G3 Plus is the first of its electric scooters to adopt a new range testing methodology intended to better reflect real-world riding.
Rather than calculating maximum range until the battery is completely depleted – when many scooters have slowed dramatically due to low battery voltage – the company now measures range until the scooter can no longer maintain at least 60% of the selected riding mode’s maximum speed. According to Segway, that provides riders with a more realistic estimate of usable range. The company even claims that while the new scooter is officially rated for six more miles than the previous MAX G3, it would have shown roughly a 12-mile improvement had both scooters been measured under the same standard.
Beyond the bigger battery, the MAX G3 Plus receives several rider-focused upgrades. New dedicated rear turn signals join the existing handlebar indicators, while redesigned brake levers and optimized reflector placement aim to improve visibility and control. Segway has also added its new Intelligent Combined Braking System (ICBS), which blends regenerative braking with the mechanical disc brakes to improve braking performance while recovering energy and reducing brake wear.
The rest of the scooter also packs in some nicer components. Riders get dual hydraulic suspension with adjustable rear damping, 11-inch self-sealing tires, traction control, anti-lock braking, Apple Find My compatibility, a 2.4-inch TFT display with navigation, automatic headlights with high and low beams, and FlashCharge technology that can recharge the battery in around four hours – or an even quicker three hours when using dual charging cables.
At 55.6 lb (25.2 kg), the scooter isn’t exactly lightweight, but that’s fairly typical for a high-performance commuter machine packing a battery this large. The 286 lb payload rating should also accommodate a wide range of riders.
The MAX G3 Plus is available for pre-order now in the US, with an introductory price of $1,149.99 before eventually rising to its $1,499.99 MSRP.  It is scheduled to begin shipping in the US on August 25 through Segway’s online store as well as retailers, including Best Buy and Amazon.
Electrek’s Take
The larger battery and added safety features are welcome improvements, but I think the most interesting part of this launch is Segway’s decision to rethink how it reports range.
Micromobility range claims have always been something of an optimistic exercise, often measured under ideal conditions that don’t reflect how people actually ride. Measuring usable range instead of “until the scooter finally crawls to a stop” feels like a much more consumer-friendly approach. If the rest of the industry follows suit, we’ll end up with specifications that are easier to compare and much more useful for riders trying to figure out whether a scooter can actually handle their daily commute.
That said, it doesn’t account for the fact that maximum ranges are nearly universally listed in the device’s lowest power setting, despite a small fraction of scooters being used in that setting. Most riders leave a scooter in its higher settings most of its life, meaning the real-world range is often significantly less than the maximum marketing claim. Thus, I always prefer to see a complete list of ranges provided for each power level, though this is a rarity in the industry. Even so, any move towards more honest range ratings is a move in the right direction.

title: Revoy hybrid tandem trailer rolls towards reality with $27 million raise
content:
Jo Borrás
| Aug 4 2026 - 4:20 am PT
Dealroom
is reporting that the San Francisco-based trucking startup raised $27 million in a Series A funding led by Standard Capital, with Doerr Capital, Time Ventures, Y Combinator, and Leap Ventures participating. The money is being earmarked to towards the development of cheaper, “second-generation” hybrid trailer dolly with a smaller battery but similar fuel economy gains.
given the questions raised about the GCWR implications of the dolly in the first place
, I’d argue that that’s
the right move for Revoy.
The timing of the raise matters, too. The company just completed a year-long proof of concept pilot with Ryder Systems,
and plans to deploy four more along a 200-mile route in the PNW by the end of this year
. “Dozens” more are set to be in operation, “by the end of 2027.”
You can read more about Revoy EV’s concept in this article from 2024,
following the trailer dolly’s regulatory approval from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
(NHTSA) back in 2023, below, then let us know what you think of the concept in the comments.
Revoy EV promises to electrify diesel semis in minutes
Hybrid electric trailer; by Revoy.
The Revoy EV concept is deceptively simple. A tractor’s 5th wheel pairs up with the Revoy’s hitch. Then the trailer that the semi is set to haul attaches to the Revoy’s 5th wheel. Some AI embedded in the Revoy’s electronic control units does some number-crunching and the three-part truck, trailer, trailer combo then hauls off down the road, with the Revoy’s high-torque e-axle providing most of the power to accelerate the load and diesel power where
most efficient: on the highway.
The best part, according to Revoy? Truckers can add the Revoy EV trailer to their rigs with no up-front costs.
“We offer a really different and much better and easier path for fleets to go electric,” offers Revoy EV’s founder, Ian Rust. “We offer a service, (zero money up front for the unit, then) customers pay us by the mile. It’s really more of a fuel product. We charge them for the diesel we save them, altogether with the residual diesel, and our fees that are all inclusive.”
The Revoy EV has a range of about 250 miles,
which comparable to the 2nd generation Volvo VNR Electric
Freightliner eCascadia models
. “On a 250-mile run, a truck getting 7 mpg might burn 35 gallons of diesel, which we’ll say costs $4/gallon or $140,”
writes Alex Lockie
the Commercial Carrier Journal
. “The Revoy EV would cut that in half, approximately, and bill the fleet for a cut of the difference.”
Revoy EV hybrid semi trailer
Revoy is launching with two “swap stations” already up and running in Texas and Arkansas, where drivers can pull into the station, be greeted by a Revoy attendant, then swap out their spent battery “in about five minutes or so,” according to the press release. Rust adds that Revoy has stations planned for California and Oregon as well.
Electrek’s Take
Revoy cutaway.
Where do we start? On the one hand, the Revoy EV is very much not vaporware. This is a thoroughly conceived, well-engineered, and seemingly well-funded effort to bring someone’s big idea to life. On the other hand, the concept itself seems deeply flawed.
The first major problem with the Revoy EV is its weight. The electrified trailer weighs in at about 22,000 pounds, according to the company – around 2,000 pounds lighter than the previously mentioned Volvo VNR Electric and as much as 6,000 pounds
than a Freightliner eCascadia.
National rules say that without a special permit, a semi-truck and the trailer it is hauling can’t collectively weigh more than 80,000 pounds in total
. Worse, the Revoy doesn’t fit into any special legal loopholes that can help make that mass go away (because the Revoy isn’t a ZEV, it doesn’t even get the extra 2,000 lb. GVWR allowance a BEV gets). That means adding a Revoy trailer to your rig effectively negates your ability to haul 22,000 lbs. of the stuff that, you know, you’re actually being
to haul.
Add in the potential safety risks and generically “weird” handling characteristics presented by adding an extra few articulations into the mix and the Revoy starts to look even more like a liability.
Still, the Revoy guys aren’t dumb – and a number of knowledgeable industry people have jumped in to defend Rust’s concept. “In high-value freight at least,” offers Lockie, “the trend has been toward the extreme majority of loads cubing out before they ever weigh out.”
Rust, to his credit, at least acknowledges the problems. “The key is when we encounter those trailers that can’t afford the weight (of the Revoy EV), we wave them on,” he says. “We looked at the data … two thirds of loads can accommodate the extra weight.”
With so many commercial fleets complaining that the 2000 lb. EV adjustment isn’t enough, I (for one) question Rust’s confidence. Still, I’m just one guy – and you, dear readers? You’re smart. Head on down to the comments and let me know what
think of the Revoy EV, and whether or not you think it’ll be a staple of trucking’s future.
